H1.text: A bicycle wheel keeps most of its weight at the rim. A machine flywheel is heavy at its edge. A grinding stone is solid all the way through.

H2.text: Same idea every time: where the mass sits changes how it spins.

H3.text: Aarav has a ring and a disc. Same mass. Same size. He gives each the same push.

H4.text: The disc whirls faster. The ring is lazier. Same mass, so why?

H5.text: To compare them in one number, we use the radius of gyration.

P1.text: Squeeze all of a body's mass into a thin ring around the axis.

P2.text: Choose the ring's radius so that its moment of inertia matches the body's.

P3.text: That radius is the radius of gyration, k. So I equals M k squared.

P4.text: k tells you how far out the mass sits, on average, in the way that counts for turning.

S1.text: Our motion notebook. A disc of mass two kilograms and radius half a metre. Its I is half M R squared. Point two five.

S2.text: Now take a ring with the same two kilograms, at the full half metre. Its I is M R squared. Point five. Too big.

S3.text: Shrink the ring. Its I falls fast, because r is squared. Watch the dot slide down the curve.

S5.text: Here the ring's I equals the disc's I. Point two five. The lines cross.

S6.text: The radius is point three five four metres. That is the disc's radius of gyration.

S7.text: It is less than the full radius, because a disc has much of its mass near the centre.

D1.text: Let's find k for a disc, step by step.

D2.text: Step one. By its meaning, I equals M k squared.

D3.text: Step two. So k equals the square root of I over M.

D4.text: Step three. For a disc about its centre, I is half M R squared. Put it in: M k squared equals half M R squared.

D5.text: Step four. Cancel M. k squared is R squared over two. So k is R over root two, about point seven R.

D6.text: Half a metre times point seven zero seven. Point three five four. The same as the sim.

T1.text: Remember this. The radius of gyration is where all the mass could sit and give the same moment of inertia.

R1.text: Now, why the disc's k is smaller, link by link.

R2.text: In a ring, every bit of mass sits at the full radius.

R3.text: In a disc, many bits sit close to the centre.

R4.text: Bits near the axis add very little, because r is squared.

R5.text: So the disc has a smaller I, and its k sits inside the rim.

C1.text: Here are the common bodies you must know, from the NCERT table.

C2.text: A ring about its central axis: M R squared. A disc: half M R squared.

C3.text: A thin rod about its middle: M L squared over twelve.

C4.text: A solid sphere about a diameter: two fifths M R squared.

K1.text: Side by side. Ring and disc, two kilograms, half a metre. Give each one joule of energy.

K2.text: The ring, with I point five, turns at two radians per second. The disc, with half the I, turns at two point eight three.

K3.text: Now you try. A solid sphere and a disc, same mass, same radius. Which has the smaller moment of inertia about a central axis? Pause and decide.

K4.text: The sphere! Two fifths is less than one half. More of a sphere's mass sits close to the axis.

K5.text: One more. A hollow cylinder and a ring, same mass, same radius, about their central axis. Which has the bigger I? Pause and decide.

K6.text: Neither! Both are M R squared. In both, every bit of mass is at the full radius. Length along the axis does not matter.

W2.text: A uniform rod is one point two metres long, with a mass of two kilograms. Find its moment of inertia and radius of gyration about its middle.

W3.text: I equals M L squared over twelve. Two times one point four four, over twelve. Point two four.

W4.text: k equals root of I over M. Root of point two four over two. Root of point one two.

W5.text: So k is about point three four six metres.

X2.text: Many students write k equals R over two for a disc.

X3.text: About its central axis, k is R over root two. R over two is only for an axis along a diameter. Always check the axis.

E1.text: Where is this asked? In ratio questions between common bodies, and in finding k from I.

Q1.text: Exam level now. A solid sphere about a diameter, and a ring about its central axis, have the same radius of gyration. Find the ratio of the sphere's radius to the ring's radius. Pause and solve.

A1.text: The answer is B. Root of five over two.

A2.text: For the ring, k equals its radius.

A3.text: For the sphere, k squared is two fifths of its radius squared.

A4.text: Set them equal. The sphere's radius over the ring's is root of five over two. About one point five eight.

F1.text: Here is your recap. Screenshot this card.

Y1.text: Can you answer these without help?

Y2.text: One. What does the radius of gyration of a body mean?

Y3.text: Two. Why is a disc's radius of gyration less than its radius?

Y4.text: Three. Why do a ring and a hollow cylinder of the same mass and radius have the same I?

N1.text: Next time: spin a coin flat, then on its edge, then about a point on its rim. Three different answers from one coin. The theorems of perpendicular and parallel axes.
